title: Daily Digest — October 15, 2026 · Technical Discovery
subtitle: Polar-metal order, 603 optical cavities, quantum timing, ESP32 post-quantum security and 30-fps e-paper
editor_note: Seven in-depth articles on new optical and condensed-matter experiments, mathematical quantum theory and practical ESP32 hardware. Original studies and engineering reports are linked and dated. Experimental measurements, theoretical predictions and author demonstrations are distinguished. The September 25 trapped-ion experiment is included as clearly dated recent research, not misrepresented as today's discovery.

articles.title: A femtosecond pulse orders a metal that should screen an electric field
articles.dek: Second-harmonic symmetry measurements resolve how local polar regions align in doped strontium titanate.
articles.timing: Kandil, Tomioka, Ren, Comes, Inoue and Jin; Physical Review Letters 137, 166801, published October 14, 2026, DOI 10.1103/nx3d-1mqf. Preprint arXiv:2608.18427, August 19. Experiment.

paragraphs.heading: Why a polar metal is a puzzle
paragraphs.text: Ferroelectric insulators carry electric dipoles whose alignment can create a macroscopic polarization. In a metal, mobile electrons screen static electric fields, complicating electrical switching and leaving an unsettled question about the underlying polar transition. Is the lattice moving collectively as a soft phonon condenses, or are nanoscale patches already polar and merely waiting to align? Both descriptions can produce a macroscopic loss of inversion symmetry. Distinguishing them requires information about local orientation statistics rather than a simple bulk current or dielectric measurement.

Kandil and colleagues studied Sr0.95Ba0.05Ti(1-x)Nb(x)O3, deliberately adding charge carriers by substituting niobium. Their reported Hall densities across selected samples were approximately 2.27 × 10^19, 5.04 × 10^19 and 3.40 × 10^20 carriers per cubic centimeter. This is not an insulating ferroelectric with a decorative label: the screening carriers are part of the phenomenon. Comparing doping helps establish whether local polar organization survives when ordinary long-range electrostatic control becomes ineffective.

paragraphs.heading: An optical symmetry meter
paragraphs.text: Their method was rotational-anisotropy second-harmonic generation, RA-SHG. The nonlinear optical polarization contains a term P(2omega) = epsilon_0 chi(2) E(omega)^2, where chi(2) is the susceptibility tensor. Illuminating at frequency omega generates light at 2omega; rotating the beam and polarization geometry selects different tensor components. Bulk electric-dipole SHG is suppressed by inversion symmetry in the simple limit, though surfaces and higher-order multipoles also contribute. What matters is therefore the angular response and its temperature dependence, fitted with the relevant symmetry model—not a simplistic count of bright spots.

According to the experimental methods, the 800-nanometer probe consisted of approximately 50-femtosecond pulses at 200 kilohertz with a spot roughly 50 micrometers across. A separate pump near 700 nanometers and 70 femtoseconds illuminated a larger region, about 80 micrometers across. The sample was measured under vacuum in a cryostat. Because the optical spot encompasses enormous numbers of nanoscale polar regions, it does not directly image individual dipoles. Instead, it measures an ensemble-sensitive optical signal; the team analyzes angular patterns as the regions appear, align, and lose alignment over thermal cycles.

paragraphs.heading: What light writes
paragraphs.text: Across the transition, the changing angular SHG patterns favor an order-disorder interpretation: nanoscale polarized regions are present and their orientations organize, rather than all polarization appearing only when a single collective displacement becomes stable. Above the transition the pump can impose a reproducible preferred orientation, and the observed texture can be reversed by optical control. This is specific experimental evidence about the orientation distribution, not proof that every microscopic force involved in the transition has been isolated. A soft lattice mode can still participate in a system whose order parameter has important local fluctuations.

The central engineering appeal is a way around electrostatic screening: use a rapid optical interaction to manipulate a polar organization in a conductor. But a femtosecond laser pulse is not equivalent to a femtosecond nonvolatile memory write. One would need independently measured retention after illumination, write energy, minimum feature size, cycling endurance, and cross-talk before suggesting a usable device. What has been achieved is an experimental separation of competing microscopic pictures, together with a reversible optical control effect observable in a symmetry-sensitive measurement.

sources.title: Optical poling of a quantum ferroelectric metal across the order-disorder phase transition

articles.title: One resonator, 603 addressable optical cavities: the scaling problem is aberration
articles.dek: The achievement is not a projected spot count but hundreds of spatially separated, nearly frequency-matched resonant optical modes.
articles.timing: Anna Soper, Danial Shadmany, Adam Shaw, Lukas Palm, David Schuster and Jonathan Simon; Physical Review X 16, 041009, published October 8, 2026, DOI 10.1103/9cwp-ppp2. Experimental cavity-array characterization.

paragraphs.heading: Why a hologram is not a quantum cavity
paragraphs.text: A trapped atom interacting with photons inside a resonator benefits from light repeatedly passing through the same small region. That can support nondestructive readout or a link between atomic and flying-photon quantum information. Scaling from one atom to hundreds traditionally invites hundreds of individually stabilized mirror pairs, a mechanical and optical calibration nightmare. A holographic beam splitter could create many laser spots, but those would not automatically enjoy resonant enhancement. The cavity-array microscope is a third architecture: optical elements inside one large mirror resonator form a two-dimensional matrix of distinct tightly focused transverse modes, each capable of addressing one site.

Soper and collaborators use mirrors roughly a meter apart, microlens optics and an intracavity geometry designed so separated fundamental-like modes coexist in the same physical resonator. They characterize 603 spatial channels. The term 'cavities' here describes the resonant modes rather than 603 separate metal boxes or mirror assemblies. A spatial light modulator selectively interrogates positions. Optical measurements determine mode shape, resonance frequency and loss. The count is a property of the characterized optical system: 603 entangled atoms, memories or quantum communications have not been demonstrated by this measurement.

paragraphs.heading: The number that matters more than 603
paragraphs.text: Resonance frequency varies with optical path length. Light at one frequency can therefore excite many sites efficiently only if their resonances overlap. The team found 537 modes mutually degenerate to within one cavity linewidth under optimized conditions. The fraction 537/603 is about 0.89, a useful derived count of spatial sites whose frequency spread permits common-frequency interrogation; it is emphatically not an entanglement fidelity. This observation is harder to achieve than drawing 603 geometrically plausible laser dots: every extra field position sees slightly different lens curvature, thickness and path length, which can move its resonance out of the shared window.

A useful quality measure is the finesse, F = FSR/delta_f: the free spectral range between longitudinal resonances divided by their linewidth. Their array-averaged measured finesse is approximately 114(17). Higher finesse corresponds to more round trips of the intracavity light, unless other factors limit the atom's interaction. As an illustration, a simple empty one-meter cavity has free spectral range c/(2L), about 150 megahertz; finesse 114 would imply a linewidth near 1.3 megahertz. This is deliberately a rough calculation for an empty two-mirror system, not the group's actual linewidth, because intracavity lenses and other optical elements alter the effective path and mode geometry.

paragraphs.heading: Where the loss and mode mismatch come from
paragraphs.text: The effective field-of-view radius is about 140 micrometers. The mode waist is approximately 1.15 micrometers, a scale compatible with individual trapped atoms. Aspheric intracavity lenses produce field-dependent aberration, and holding their positions sufficiently constant requires transverse tolerances of order hundreds of nanometers and longitudinal control around ten micrometers in sensitive configurations. Those tolerances explain why a visually well-aligned setup could still have large resonance-frequency variation. The paper examines lens losses, optical surface contamination and antireflection coating limits; the aspheric elements account for much of the loss budget. Their effect is multiplied by the number of round trips. A little scattered light per pass becomes a strong limit on finesse.

This is one of the most generalizable lessons in the work: a shared component imposes a correlated impairment on every otherwise separate logical channel. The additional modes are not free. The single optical system has to be designed to preserve frequency degeneracy and mode quality over an expanding field. The team's analysis of wide-field objectives suggests a path toward more than 17,000 sites, but that figure is a projected optical design, not measured hardware. Likewise, useful large-scale atom–photon operation would need reliable trapping, site-selective calibration, low-loss photon collection, phase stability and measured photon indistinguishability. The experiment has established an impressive resonator architecture and a quantified route for engineering it further, not a complete quantum network.

articles.title: What looks like an attosecond electron delay may instead be a property of light
articles.dek: Theoretical photoelectron interference separates atomic emission timing from the phase carried by nonclassical photon-number correlations.
articles.timing: Liding Li, Xu Zhang, Shouyu Xiao, Yang Li, Peixiang Lu and Yueming Zhou; Physical Review Letters 137, 163201, published October 13, 2026, DOI 10.1103/qygr-6xcg. Theoretical prediction, not a reported experiment.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring time by measuring phase
paragraphs.text: An attosecond pump–probe experiment rarely involves starting and stopping a literal clock. In the RABBIT method, an extreme-ultraviolet pulse train ejects electrons and a time-delayed infrared field changes their measured energy. An electron in a selected spectral sideband can reach that final energy by absorbing an infrared photon along one path or emitting a photon along another. Both pathways end in the same electron energy state, so their complex amplitudes interfere. The number of electrons in that sideband oscillates with probe delay tau, approximately I(tau) = A + B cos(2 omega tau + phi), where omega is the infrared angular frequency and phi the measured interference phase. After correcting known optical contributions, experimenters interpret part of that phase as a photoemission time delay.

The interpretation normally assumes that the probe light is well described by a coherent classical-like field. But quantum optics also supplies squeezed states: light with fluctuations deliberately redistributed between complementary field quadratures. Two beams with similar intensity can have distinctly different number correlations and phase-sensitive quantum properties. Li and colleagues mathematically replaced the conventional probe with squeezed-vacuum light and calculated how electrons would respond. They found that the statistics of photons in the driving field can leave an additional phase signature in the electron sidebands. If an observer attributes the entire phase to electron motion, the inferred difference can be several tens of attoseconds.

paragraphs.heading: What an anomalous moment measures
paragraphs.text: In quantized-field notation, the annihilation operator a removes one photon from a mode and the creation operator a-dagger adds one. The ordinary mean photon number is <a-dagger a>. But the complex quantity <a squared> measures a pair correlation, including a phase that photon counting alone may not reveal. The proposed photoelectron interference is sensitive to the phase of that second-order anomalous moment. Extending the analysis to a three-sideband arrangement allows access to a fourth-order moment, <a to the fourth>, and greater sensitivity to certain quantum fluctuations. This is an unusual way for matter waves to act as a phase-sensitive detector of properties of the light that produced them.

paragraphs.heading: How big is a ten-attosecond phase?
paragraphs.text: The conversion between an extra fringe phase delta_phi and an apparent delay is delta_tau = delta_phi/(2 omega). For a derived scale example, the frequency of 800-nanometer light is approximately 375 terahertz, so omega is about 2.36 × 10^15 radians per second. A phase perturbation of 0.1 radian then corresponds to roughly 21 attoseconds of inferred delay. This calculation is only a unit conversion; it does not reproduce a particular data point from the paper. It also exposes a measurement pitfall: a change in the probe's quantum state can masquerade as a change in an atom's timing if the extra field-dependent phase is omitted.

The paper provides a theoretical protocol, not an experiment where a squeezed infrared probe has already been shown to resolve those anomalous moments on an attosecond scale. A credible demonstration would have to characterize the probe state independently, compare coherent and squeezed controls, and separate normal atomic continuum–continuum delays from the quantum-light term. Its value is a testable extension to the interpretation of a mature interferometer. It says not that photoemission takes extra physical time whenever quantum light is used, but that the same electron-fringe observable can encode more than one kind of phase.

articles.title: The Born rule's hidden assumption: probabilities must add
articles.dek: A mathematical comparison of famous quantum-probability derivations asks what is already being assumed before the squared-amplitude rule appears.
articles.timing: Jiaxuan Zhang; Physical Review A 114, 042208, published October 13, 2026, DOI 10.1103/mqy7-s2db. Mathematical analysis; earlier preprint arXiv:2603.06211 submitted March 2026.

paragraphs.heading: Why squaring amplitudes is another rule
paragraphs.text: Quantum mechanics computes complex amplitudes for possible measurement outcomes. It then maps those amplitudes to observed probabilities through the Born rule: for a normalized state |psi> and a measurement projector P, the probability is <psi|P|psi>. For a two-state superposition alpha|0> + beta|1>, the measurement probabilities are |alpha| squared and |beta| squared. The unitary equations tell us how alpha and beta evolve, but do not immediately tell us why the probability should be that function rather than some other nonlinear assignment. Several foundational programs try to derive it from apparently more basic principles.

paragraphs.heading: The small word with a large consequence
paragraphs.text: Additivity is the rule that probabilities of mutually exclusive alternatives sum: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) when A and B cannot occur together. Countable additivity extends the formula to a countably infinite set of disjoint alternatives. These constraints are more informative than simply insisting that a collection of probabilities be nonnegative and sum to one. They connect the probabilities assigned to individual detector clicks with the probability assigned when those clicks are deliberately grouped into a coarse-grained detector bin. A proposed probability mapping might normalize correctly for one basis yet fail to agree with the same experiment described through a different grouping.

Zhang compares several celebrated derivations, including Gleason-style measures over projectors, extensions of the projection logic, decision-theoretic Everettian arguments, and environment-assisted derivations. The study argues that explicit or effectively equivalent forms of additivity do indispensable work in the derivations examined. For instance, if orthogonal projectors describe disjoint alternatives, a probability measure consistent across decompositions requires their weights to combine in a certain way. Decision-theoretic approaches likewise need consistency conditions for composing games or branching choices. Such conditions can be reasonable, but deriving a rule from them does not establish those premises independently as laws of nature.

paragraphs.heading: A deliberately wrong rule makes the issue visible
paragraphs.text: Imagine a three-outcome state with amplitudes alpha, beta and gamma. One could invent weights proportional to |alpha| to the fourth, |beta| to the fourth and |gamma| to the fourth, divided by their total so the assigned probabilities sum to one. This is a mathematical counterexample to the idea that normalization alone selects the square law; it is not a plausible experimental alternative to quantum theory. Demanding consistency under coarse-graining and under changes of basis adds constraints that can rule out such recipes. The precise hypotheses of a theorem are therefore the substance of the derivation, not legalistic fine print.

The paper is not new evidence for a violation of the Born rule and does not settle competing interpretations of wavefunction collapse or Everettian branches. Its contribution is a sharper inventory of logical dependencies in attempts to establish the familiar rule. Even a rigorous theorem leaves a distinct physical question: why should the real experiment obey the premises of that theorem? The transferable insight extends beyond quantum foundations. When a surprising result follows from a 'minimal' set of axioms, ask whether a strong version of the conclusion was hidden in a consistency or composition assumption.

sources.title: Summing to Uncertainty: On the Necessity of Additivity in Deriving the Born Rule

articles.title: Post-quantum cryptography on ESP32: large signatures and the real boot trust boundary
articles.dek: Espressif's new experimental software component makes ML-KEM and ML-DSA measurable on actual microcontrollers, without pretending the hardware is quantum-proof.
articles.timing: Pranav Sonawane for Espressif Developer Portal, October 14, 2026; original Espressif esp-pqc repository and example documentation inspected. Hardware benchmarks are vendor-reported.

paragraphs.heading: Key exchange and signatures are different problems
paragraphs.text: A long-lived embedded device uses public-key cryptography to establish private sessions and to authenticate firmware or servers. Espressif's esp-pqc component adds software implementations of NIST ML-KEM, a lattice-based key-encapsulation mechanism, and ML-DSA, a lattice-based signature scheme, to ESP-IDF. The bundled mbedTLS override demonstrates TLS 1.3 hybrid X25519MLKEM768 key exchange: the ordinary elliptic-curve X25519 exchange and a post-quantum shared secret both contribute to the session key. ML-DSA-65 certificates can separately authenticate the peer. A key encapsulation is not a signature and neither one alone delivers both confidentiality and authenticated software updates.

paragraphs.heading: Protocol size is not incidental
paragraphs.text: In the example, a standalone X25519 key share requires 32 bytes, while the hybrid key share consumes 1,216 bytes. That is 38 times as much key-share data before packet framing. An ML-DSA-65 public key is 1,952 bytes and its signature 3,309 bytes. The sample CA certificate is 7,571 bytes. A device that allocates TLS buffers on internal SRAM rather than external PSRAM can discover that what looked like a simple crypto-library upgrade changes its worst-case heap demand. On a fragmented Wi-Fi link, larger handshake records also require more packets, retransmission opportunities and CPU time. The security algorithm and the protocol transport cannot be budgeted independently.

The repository offers liboqs-derived algorithms behind OQS_KEM and OQS_SIG APIs plus an mbedTLS override. It requires ESP-IDF version 6.0 or newer. Its platform table lists ESP32, S2, S3, C-series, H2 and P4, but that does not mean every example supports every chip: the hybrid TLS demonstration needs suitable network support and flash, while its experimental additional boot signature verifier targets C3, C5 and C6. No current ESP32 in this implementation accelerates ML-KEM or ML-DSA in dedicated hardware. The new arithmetic runs as software on the host CPU.

paragraphs.heading: The secure-boot chain cannot be wished away
paragraphs.text: In a secure-boot design, the verifier itself must be protected by an earlier trusted stage. An attacker who can simply replace both the application and its verifier can make any software signature rule irrelevant. The project's boot example adds an ML-DSA-65 verification at the second-stage bootloader, while retaining the ordinary hardware-rooted classical Secure Boot V2 mechanism. This is an *additional* post-quantum authorization check, not a rewritten mask ROM, post-quantum eFuse storage or a hardware mechanism to revoke post-quantum private keys. The app acquires an additional signature block of about 8 kilobytes, on top of the classical four-kilobyte signature sector.

paragraphs.heading: Measured overhead on an 80-megahertz ESP32-C5
paragraphs.text: Espressif reports roughly 30 milliseconds to hash the relevant image and classical sector using the SHA accelerator, 44 milliseconds to verify ML-DSA-65 in software, and 13 milliseconds for an RSA-PSS-3072 verification using the hardware accelerator. With integration overhead, the total hybrid boot verification measured approximately 91 milliseconds. A separate TLS experiment completed a hybrid handshake in roughly 300 milliseconds including network round trips. That figure must not be advertised as the standalone ML-KEM time: network latency, certificate length and buffering conditions all contribute. The blog also records different signature verification timing between a FreeRTOS application and a bootloader, which makes benchmark context indispensable.

The project's README is explicit: esp-pqc is for experimentation and evaluation, not production. It has no eFuse-backed storage or hardware revocation path for post-quantum keys, and it needs implementation-specific side-channel assessment. Example credentials must never be deployed as live signing keys. What has been achieved is a reproducible point from which developers can inspect hybrid TLS traffic, measure heap and stack peaks, and benchmark signature verification under their own hardware conditions. It provides a concrete engineering route for planning quantum-resistant migrations, while leaving the trust-anchor and production-hardening problems visibly unfinished.

articles.title: Thirty frames a second on a 1.54-inch e-paper screen: controlled ghosting as grayscale
articles.dek: A Game Boy prototype trades complete pixel settling for calibrated short pulses on an ESP32-S3-controlled electrophoretic panel.
articles.timing: Tyler August, Hackaday, October 14, 2026, reporting Bo Made It's Waveshare ESP32-S3-ePaper-1.54 prototype. Demonstrated by its author on video; source code was not public at the reporting cutoff.

paragraphs.heading: The slow refresh is partly a driving policy
paragraphs.text: An ordinary e-paper page refresh is designed to make a stable, clean, high-contrast image, not to produce the fastest possible sequence of game frames. Charged pigment particles must move through a fluid under electric fields, and the screen's history affects where they start. Standard controller waveforms include several voltage phases to reduce residual charge and ghosting. On a tiny 1.54-inch Waveshare ESP32-S3 e-paper board, developer Bo Made It reports a Game Boy emulator running at 30 frames per second by replacing the conventional full-settling update strategy with much shorter, pixel-selective drive sequences. Hackaday covered the demonstration on October 14.

paragraphs.heading: Think of each pixel as retaining state
paragraphs.text: The unusual trick is to use the persistence that usually makes electrophoretic panels annoying. Instead of commanding every pixel to become pure black or white on each frame, the controller records which transitions are desired and applies a limited number of drive pulses. Reporting describes a per-pixel budget up to eight pulses depending on how far that pixel needs to move. For a gray transition, an intentionally incomplete move becomes a reproducible intermediate reflectance. The software must distinguish dark-to-light from light-to-dark and must know the previous state: pixel response is not a memoryless mapping from a two-bit value to a voltage.

A Game Boy image conventionally has 160 × 144 visible pixels and four grayscale levels. Four shades can be encoded in two bits, but an electrophoretic display that only offers reliable binary endpoints needs an experimentally determined transition table to reproduce them. With four possible old shades and four targets there are sixteen ordered pairs, twelve of which represent an actual color change. A transition from black to light gray need not take the same pulse time or polarity as light gray to black. The developer used iterative visual recording and calibration to refine those transitions. The much larger set of voltage histories is why a fast display demo often succeeds before a generally stable driver exists.

paragraphs.heading: A frame budget is not a quality guarantee
paragraphs.text: At 30 frames per second, each frame spans about 33.3 milliseconds. That is the wall-clock budget for emulation, framebuffer updates, data transfer, controller commands and any chosen pixel pulses. It does not mean the individual pigment particles physically settled into a final stable state in 33 milliseconds. The observed animation and apparent four-shade fidelity are trade-offs between short-term contrast, residue from previous frames and transition-specific drive sequences. Static reading pages need a different objective: high contrast, minimal ghosting and controlled long-term appearance. A fast animation driver should typically offer a subsequent settling or cleanup path rather than using the same short waveform forever.

Hackaday emphasizes an important hardware distinction from earlier high-frame-rate projects: this prototype goes through the board's existing waveform-capable e-paper controller, rather than driving bare panel electrodes directly. That means its improvement is a firmware and controller-command discovery on accessible hardware. However, the source repository is not yet public and the exact waveform table, thermal dependence, power draw and long-term pigment wear have not been independently assessed. A quoted 30 fps is an author-demonstrated throughput result, not a full characterization of image quality under all content or temperatures. The transferable idea is explicit modeling of each pixel's physical history rather than treating it as a binary, instantaneous display element.

articles.title: Two ions simulate how a quantum flux blocks matter tunnelling
articles.dek: A hybrid spin-and-vibration system makes gauge fields dynamic, instead of merely programming a particle's background force.
articles.timing: Saner and collaborators, Nature Physics, September 25, 2026; DOI 10.1038/s41567-026-03400-6. Peer-reviewed trapped-ion experiment, selected as a deeper recent study rather than new October 15 news.

paragraphs.text: In a gauge theory, the field that mediates an interaction must evolve with the matter it influences. Representing a moving particle in a fixed external potential is easier, but it omits the feedback between charge and field as well as the local constraints of gauge symmetry. S. Saner and colleagues at Oxford, working with collaborators, built a small trapped-ion machine in which different physical degrees of freedom represent those components. The two-level internal states of ions serve as gauge links; their quantized collective vibrations serve as bosonic matter sites. This is a useful hybrid: an oscillator can store several occupation levels without allocating separate binary qubits for every possible matter excitation.

The model uses the Z2 gauge group, meaning a link has two possible signed configurations. Multiplying link signs around a closed path defines a flux-like quantity, and a matter particle moving along alternative routes can accumulate a relative sign. This is not quantum chromodynamics—the group here is discrete, not the continuous non-Abelian symmetry of the strong interaction. But it captures a hard feature that toy simulations commonly remove: matter and the link field are quantum variables that evolve together under rules analogous to Gauss's law.

The researchers designed laser-driven interactions between spin and motion to realize state-dependent transfer of excitation between oscillator modes. Digital gates prepare states, including entangled link states; analogue evolution produces the time dependence of the engineered Hamiltonian. Because connectivity is synthesized through couplings between modes, the 'lattice' does not need to be a literal array of atoms laid out as a square. One trapped ion can supply an elementary link. Two ions, with two selected normal modes and two link qubits, can form the smallest useful closed loop in a synthetic spatial dimension.

The elementary-link measurements established correlated changes in matter occupation and the gauge variable. In a zero-field limit the paper reports a fitted tunnelling parameter J/pi = 1.510(6) kHz; the parenthetical notation means a statistical uncertainty of 0.006 kHz in the quoted digits. Increasing the programmed electric field changed oscillation rate and suppressed the charge-transfer amplitude. Numerical models with independently calibrated parameters reproduced broad behavior, while deviations from simple analytic expectations were associated with the effective electric field being smaller than the nominal setting. The experiment tests an implemented Hamiltonian with imperfections, not a mathematical Hamiltonian materialized without error.

The more revealing configuration is the two-link loop. The investigators prepared different entangled states for the two gauge qubits: one encodes no effective magnetic flux, the other encodes a pi flux, sometimes called a Z2 vison. Matter can tunnel between the two vibrational sites by two distinguishable routes before the amplitudes are recombined. In the zero-flux sector, occupation oscillated between sites and the fitted loop tunnelling rate was about J/pi = 0.35 kHz. In the pi-flux sector, transfer was strongly inhibited. The flux is an encoded quantum property of entangled ion spins, not a physical magnetic coil threaded through an actual electron circuit.

A simple interference calculation explains the switch. If two paths contribute equal complex amplitudes a and a exp(i phi), the total is a[1 + exp(i phi)]. Its probability is proportional to 2 |a|^2[1 + cos(phi)]. At relative phase zero, paths reinforce; at phase pi, they cancel. This deliberately simplified two-path derivation leaves out the coupled gauge operators and decoherence, but makes the observation intelligible. The experiment does not merely alter the height of an energy barrier. It changes a gauge-flux configuration that reverses the relative phase of alternatives, which controls whether transfer occurs.

Observables came from repeated projective readouts of matter occupation and gauge-link state. In the published loop plots, post-selection left at least 64 accepted matter shots and at least 203 accepted link shots per displayed data point depending on setting, with 68% confidence intervals; the comparison model includes heating and spin decoherence. Those figures describe finite statistical evidence, not a universal demonstration of error-free simulation. No quantum advantage over classical simulation of large many-body gauge systems is claimed by this tiny example. Scaling requires more controllable modes, more gauge links, and continued satisfaction of local constraints under noise.

The established Aharonov–Bohm effect is not new. The advance is an experimental test of its interference mechanism in a deliberately built *dynamical* lattice-gauge setting using a compact hybrid processor. For a reader familiar with embedded systems, there is an appealing design analogy: rather than assigning every logical state to an interchangeable generic element, map distinct logical degrees of freedom onto physical resources best suited to them. Spin provides a discrete switch, vibration a natural multi-level excitation; controlled coupling supplies the computation.

sources.title: Aharonov–Bohm interference in a Z2 lattice gauge theory on a hybrid qubit–oscillator quantum computer
